questions.question: What is React and why does it exist? It is a library for building UIs from reusable components, using a virtual DOM and one-way data flow to keep complex interfaces predictable.
questions.title: React Core Fundamentals
questions.direct_answer: React is a JavaScript library for building user interfaces from reusable components, using a virtual DOM and unidirectional data flow to keep complex interfaces predictable. It exists because building large interactive UIs by directly manipulating the DOM (jQuery-style) becomes unmaintainable: state and view drift, events tangle, and the code resists change. React's model — describe the UI as a function of state, let it compute the diff and update the DOM — scales to large apps because the mental model is 'UI = f(state)', and the developer thinks in transformations, not DOM mutations.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand React's core model — UI as a function of state, the virtual DOM + reconciliation, components/props, state/hooks, and one-way data flow — not just how to write a component.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Memorizing hooks (useState, useEffect) without explaining the UI = f(state) model, the virtual DOM, or why one-way data flow matters.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Frame React's core as UI = f(state): components render from state/props, the virtual DOM + reconciliation diff and update the DOM, hooks manage state/effects, and one-way data flow keeps it predictable.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content: React is a JavaScript library for building user interfaces from reusable components, using a virtual DOM and unidirectional data flow to keep complex interfaces predictable. It exists because building large interactive UIs by directly manipulating the DOM (jQuery-style) becomes unmaintainable: state and view drift, events tangle, and the code resists change. React's model — describe the UI as a function of state, let it compute the diff and update the DOM — scales to large apps because the mental model is 'UI = f(state)', and the developer thinks in transformations, not DOM mutations. The core runtime is the virtual DOM and reconciliation: render a tree, diff against the previous, apply the minimal DOM update.

sections.title: Core Concepts
sections.content: The core ideas: (1) UI = f(state) — a component is a function of its state and props that returns the view; React keeps the DOM in sync with that output; (2) the virtual DOM and reconciliation — React renders a lightweight tree, diffs it against the previous, and applies the minimal change to the real DOM (the Fiber algorithm); (3) components and props — components are reusable, composable units; props are inputs passed down (immutable); (4) state and hooks — useState (local state), useEffect (side effects), useMemo/useCallback (memoization), useContext (shared state); hooks let function components hold state and effects; (5) one-way data flow — data flows down via props, actions flow up via callbacks; this makes the flow traceable; (6) keys for lists — stable keys identify list items so reconciliation can match them across renders; (7) re-render triggers — state/props change, parent re-renders, context changes.

sections.title: React Core Concepts and Their Roles
A component, state, an effect, and one-way data flow
Trade-offs & When It Matters
sections.content: The central tension is the declarative model versus direct control: React's 'UI = f(state)' is predictable at scale but abstracts away the DOM, which frustrates fine-grained control and performance tuning; the escape hatches (useRef, useMemo, React.memo) exist but are overused (premature optimization). A second tension: useEffect is powerful but a common source of bugs (stale closures, missing deps, infinite loops); the React team now teaches 'don't sync effects, derive state' and useSyncExternalStore for external state. The third: the virtual DOM is not free — large trees diff every render; React's answer is React Server Components and concurrent rendering to reduce client work.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: React's core model is UI = f(state) — components render from state/props, React diffs and updates the DOM — think in transformations, not DOM mutations.
The virtual DOM + reconciliation (Fiber) diffs the rendered tree against the previous and applies the minimal DOM update.
Components + props are reusable, composable units; props are immutable inputs passed down.
State + hooks (useState, useEffect, useMemo, useContext) let function components hold state and side effects — mind effect deps and stale closures.
One-way data flow: data down via props, actions up via callbacks — makes the flow traceable at scale.
Use stable keys for lists (a real id, not array index) so reconciliation matches items across reorders.

sections.title: Spoken Answer
sections.content: React is a JavaScript library for building user interfaces from reusable components, using a virtual DOM and unidirectional data flow to keep complex interfaces predictable. It exists because building large interactive UIs by directly manipulating the DOM becomes unmaintainable — state and view drift, events tangle, and the code resists change. The mental model I stress is UI equals a function of state: a component is a function of its state and props that returns the view, and React keeps the DOM in sync with that output — you think in transformations, not DOM mutations. The core runtime is the virtual DOM and reconciliation: React renders a lightweight tree, diffs it against the previous one with the Fiber algorithm, and applies the minimal change to the real DOM. Components and props are the reusable, composable units, where props are immutable inputs passed down. State and hooks let function components hold state and side effects — useState for local state, useEffect for syncing with the outside world, and the common bugs there are stale closures and missing dependency-array values, which is why the React team now teaches to derive state where possible rather than sync with effects. One-way data flow — data down via props, actions up via callbacks — makes the flow traceable at scale. And I always stress stable keys for lists, a real id not the array index, so reconciliation matches items across reorders. The honest tension is that the declarative model abstracts away the DOM, which frustrates fine-grained control, and the escape hatches like useRef and useMemo are overused — the virtual DOM is not free, which is why React Server Components and concurrent rendering exist.

questions.question: How does the useState hook work? Explain batching and lazy initialization.
questions.title: useState Hook Explained — Updates, Batching & Lazy Init
questions.direct_answer: `useState` lets a function component remember a value across renders. You call it once with an initial value and get back a `[value, setter]` tuple — calling the setter schedules a re-render, and the next render sees the new value (it does **not** mutate `value` in place). Two non-obvious bits: pass a function — `useState(() => parseJSON(...))` — when the initial value is expensive, so React only runs it on the first render; and in React 18, multiple setter calls in the same event tick (including inside promises and timeouts) are automatically batched into a single render.

interviewer_intent.testing: Setter triggers re-render, functional updater for stale closures, lazy init () => expensiveInit(), automatic batching in React 18
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Reading state right after setState and expecting the new value — state updates are asynchronous; use the updater or an effect
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Walk through React 18's automatic batching (all events batched), lazy-init benefits, and the setState(prev => ...) pattern for avoiding stale closures

sections.title: What `useState` actually does
How a `setState` call flows through React
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Render N] --> B["useState(0) returns [value, setter]"]
    B --> C[Event handler fires]
    C --> D["setter(next)"]
    D --> E{Object.is value === next?}
    E -- yes --> F[bail out, no re-render]
    E -- no --> G[Schedule update]
    G --> H[Render N+1]
    H --> I[useState returns updated value]
```

The `Object.is` check is why setting state to the same primitive value is a no-op — React skips the render entirely. It's also why setting a *new* object literal that's structurally equal still re-renders: `Object.is({a:1}, {a:1})` is `false`.

sections.title: Lazy initialization — pass a function for expensive defaults
sections.content:
If your initial value is cheap (a number, an empty array), pass it directly. If it's expensive — parsing a big JSON blob from `localStorage`, generating a UUID, building a lookup map — wrap it in a function:

```jsx
const [user, setUser] = useState(() => JSON.parse(localStorage.getItem('user')));
```

The difference matters because the function form runs **only on the first render**. The plain form runs the expression on *every* render — React just throws away the result after the first one, but the work still happens.

| Form | When the work runs | Use when |
|---|---|---|
| `useState(value)` | Every render (result discarded after first) | Value is a literal or already cheap |
| `useState(() => compute())` | First render only | `compute()` is expensive or has side effects (e.g. `localStorage`) |

A quick smell test: if the argument is anything heavier than a literal or a prop, prefer the function form.

sections.title: The classic trap — reading state right after setting it
Automatic batching — what changed in React 18
When to reach for `useState` vs `useReducer` vs `useRef`
sections.content:
| You need... | Reach for | Why |
|---|---|---|
| One or two independent values | `useState` | Simple, ergonomic, no boilerplate |
| Multiple values that update together with branching logic | `useReducer` | Centralised transitions, easier to test, predictable in concurrent rendering |
| A mutable value that should **not** trigger re-renders (DOM node, interval id, latest callback) | `useRef` | Refs persist across renders without scheduling work |
| Cross-tree shared state | `useState` lifted to context, or a store (Zustand, Redux) | Local state shouldn't travel through props for 5+ levels |

sections.title: Pitfalls that bite in production
sections.content:
- **Calling `useState` conditionally** — inside `if`, loops, or after an early return. Breaks the call-order invariant; React mismatches state slots between renders.
- **Reading state right after setting it** and expecting the new value. Use the updater function or an effect that runs after the next render.
- **Storing derived data in state** — `const [fullName, setFullName] = useState(...)` when `firstName` and `lastName` are also state. Compute it during render instead; one less thing to keep in sync.
- **`useState(expensiveCompute())`** instead of `useState(() => expensiveCompute())`. The expensive call runs every render; React just throws away the result after the first.
- **Mutating the existing value** — `state.push(item); setState(state)`. The `Object.is` check sees the same reference and skips the re-render. Always create a new array/object: `setState([...state, item])`.

sections.title: Key points
sections.content:
- `useState(initial)` returns `[value, setter]`; the setter schedules a re-render — it does not mutate `value` in place.
- Reading state right after `setState(...)` returns the **old** value. State only updates on the next render.
- Use `setX(prev => ...)` whenever the next value depends on the previous one, especially inside async code.
- For expensive defaults, pass a function: `useState(() => parseJSON(localStorage))` — runs only on first render.
- React 18 batches all setters in the same event tick (including inside promises and timeouts) into one render.
- Setting a value `Object.is`-equal to the current one short-circuits the re-render entirely.

sections.title: How to answer this verbally
sections.content:
`useState` is the most basic React hook — it's how you give a function component its own piece of memory.

The reason it exists is that a function component is literally just a function. It runs top-to-bottom, returns some JSX, and then the variables inside it disappear. So if you want the component to remember something — a counter, a form input, whether a modal is open — you can't just use a regular variable, because it resets on every render. `useState` is React's way of saying: I'll hold this value for you between renders, and give it back next time the component runs.

The basic shape looks like this — `const [count, setCount] = useState(0)`. The argument is the initial value, used only on the first render. The return is a pair: the current value, and a setter you call to change it. Calling `setCount(count + 1)` doesn't update `count` in place — it tells React, 'on the next render of this component, count should be 1 instead of 0', and React schedules that re-render. On the next render, `useState(0)` returns 1, not 0 again.

The most common bug here is reading state right after setting it. `setCount(1); console.log(count)` still logs the old value, because state updates are queued, not synchronous — the variable in your current scope still points to the old snapshot. The fix is the functional form, `setCount(c => c + 1)`. Instead of capturing the current `count` from this render's closure, the setter receives whatever the latest queued value is — which matters a lot inside async code like timers or fetches.

The second piece is lazy initialization. If the initial value is expensive to compute — say, parsing JSON out of `localStorage` — you don't want that running on every render. Instead of `useState(parseJSON(...))`, which actually runs the parse on every render and just throws away the result after the first, you wrap it in a function: `useState(() => parseJSON(...))`. React calls that function only on the first render.

And the last piece is automatic batching, which is what changed in React 18. If you call multiple setters in the same event tick — even inside a promise or a `setTimeout` — React groups them into a single re-render. So `setName('A'); setEmail('B'); setSaved(true)` becomes one render, not three. Before React 18, batching only worked inside React event handlers, so async code would re-render once per setter and you'd sometimes see a brief flicker between intermediate states. The new behaviour is what most people expect by default.

questions.question: How does useEffect work? Explain dependencies, cleanup, and common bugs.
questions.title: useEffect Hook Explained — Dependencies, Cleanup & Pitfalls
questions.direct_answer:
How does useEffect work? Explain dependencies, cleanup, and common bugs.

**In one line:** name the mechanism, where it applies (the framework runtime (render, reconciliation, DI, CD) and the browser), and the user-visible outcome.

**Interviewers dig into:** Effect runs after paint, deps array controls re-run, cleanup runs on unmount and before next effect, Strict Mode double-invoke in dev.

**Classic weak answer:** Omitting deps causing stale closures, or passing unstable functions/objects causing infinite re-runs.

**Senior finish:** Cover deps lint rule, useCallback/useMemo to stabilize deps, and React 18 Strict Mode double-effect in dev to surface cleanup bugs.

interviewer_intent.testing: Effect runs after paint, deps array controls re-run, cleanup runs on unmount and before next effect, Strict Mode double-invoke in dev
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Omitting deps causing stale closures, or passing unstable functions/objects causing infinite re-runs
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Cover deps lint rule, useCallback/useMemo to stabilize deps, and React 18 Strict Mode double-effect in dev to surface cleanup bugs

sections.title: Why this question matters
sections.content:
This question — **useEffect Hook Explained — Dependencies, Cleanup & Pitfalls** — shows up constantly in **frontend / fullstack** interviews because it separates candidates who memorized docs from candidates who can **reason about real systems**.

**Restate the prompt:** How does useEffect work? Explain dependencies, cleanup, and common bugs.

A gold-level answer does four things in order:

1. **Define** the terms in plain English (what it is / what problem it solves).
2. **Explain the mechanism** (what runs when: browser, bundler, framework, network).
3. **Compare trade-offs** (speed vs correctness vs security vs DX) with **when you would not use** the default.
4. **Ground it in production** — caching, auth, observability, tests, or an incident you handled.

Interviewers are listening for: **Effect runs after paint, deps array controls re-run, cleanup runs on unmount and before next effect, Strict Mode double-invoke in dev**.

The fastest way to lose points is: **Omitting deps causing stale closures, or passing unstable functions/objects causing infinite re-runs**.

If you only add one “senior” layer, make it: **Cover deps lint rule, useCallback/useMemo to stabilize deps, and React 18 Strict Mode double-effect in dev to surface cleanup bugs**.

sections.title: Deep dive — what to say
sections.content:
### What to explain (middle of the answer)

- **Core mechanics:** Effect runs after paint, deps array controls re-run, cleanup runs on unmount and before next effect, Strict Mode double-invoke in dev
- **Concrete shape:** give a small code or config snippet *only if it clarifies* (5–15 lines max).
- **Interviewer follow-ups:** expect “what breaks in production?”, “how do you debug?”, “what would you measure?” — answer them proactively.

### How to sound senior (without rambling)

- Tie the feature to **user-visible outcomes** (performance, accessibility, security).
- Mention **one failure mode** you have actually seen (race, stale cache, hydration mismatch, flaky test).
- Close with **one decision rule** (“choose X when …; choose Y when …”).

sections.title: Trade-offs & senior signal
sections.content:
### Trade-offs interviewers expect you to name

- **Speed vs safety** (types, runtime checks, validation).
- **DX vs constraints** (framework magic vs explicit wiring).
- **SEO / first paint vs interactivity** (SSR/SSG/CSR choices where relevant).
- **Security vs convenience** (tokens, cookies, localStorage, third-party scripts).

### What “book answer” misses

- **Book answer:** repeats definitions.
- **Strong answer:** names **omitting deps causing stale closures, or passing unstable functions/objects causing infinite re-runs** and what you do instead.

questions.question: What is the difference between useEffect and useLayoutEffect?
questions.title: useEffect vs useLayoutEffect — When to Use Each
questions.direct_answer:
What is the difference between useEffect and useLayoutEffect?

**In one line:** name the mechanism, where it applies (the framework runtime (render, reconciliation, DI, CD) and the browser), and the user-visible outcome.

**Interviewers dig into:** useEffect runs after paint (non-blocking); useLayoutEffect runs synchronously after DOM updates but before paint (blocking); use the latter only for layout measurement.

**Classic weak answer:** Using useLayoutEffect by default — it blocks paint; useEffect is the correct default.

**Senior finish:** Mention SSR warnings for useLayoutEffect (no DOM on server), and useInsertionEffect for CSS-in-JS libs.

interviewer_intent.testing: useEffect runs after paint (non-blocking); useLayoutEffect runs synchronously after DOM updates but before paint (blocking); use the latter only for layout measurement
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using useLayoutEffect by default — it blocks paint; useEffect is the correct default
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention SSR warnings for useLayoutEffect (no DOM on server), and useInsertionEffect for CSS-in-JS libs
